Safeguarding and Thresholds of Need in Birmingham: A Practical Guide for Staff

A plain-English guide to safeguarding basics, Birmingham's Right Help, Right Time layers of need, responding to a disclosure and recording concerns, for staff working with children and young people in England.

By Gibson Nyendwa · 29 October 2026 · 6 min read

SEND & Inclusive Education: Special Educational Needs and Disabilities.

Safeguarding is part of everyone's job when you work with children and young people. This guide is adapted from my short SEND Life Transition video, Foundations of Safeguarding and Thresholds of Need, which gives an overview of a longer training session for professionals supporting children, young people and families.

It is written for Teaching Assistants, tutors, SENCOs and other staff, and for parents and carers who want to understand how the system works. It applies to England. The thresholds section describes Birmingham's own framework: other local areas use their own threshold documents, so check the one for the area where the child lives.

I have checked the guidance against the current versions: Keeping children safe in education 2026, in force in schools and colleges in England since 1 September 2026, and Birmingham's Right Help, Right Time guidance, Version 7, June 2026. Where the video simplifies something, I have added the detail below.

What safeguarding means

Keeping children safe in education (KCSIE), the Department for Education's statutory guidance for schools and colleges, defines safeguarding as more than protecting children from harm. It includes helping as soon as problems emerge, preventing harm to children's mental and physical health or development, and making sure children grow up with safe and effective care. Its core principle is simple: safeguarding is everyone's responsibility.

The video introduces four words that come up again and again.

  • Safeguarding: protecting children's welfare.
  • Resilience: a child's ability to bounce back from difficult experiences.
  • Collaboration: agencies working together and sharing information.
  • Universal services: services available to everyone, such as health and education.

Professional curiosity and the child's lived experience

Professional curiosity means looking beyond the first explanation to understand what is really happening for a child and their family. In the video I describe it as going beyond surface-level assumptions, listening to the child's lived experience (what their daily life is actually like) and challenging discrimination.

Birmingham's guidance makes the same point in its principles: understand the child's lived experience, talk and listen to children and families as early as possible, and recognise disadvantage and discrimination. KCSIE adds that children may not feel ready or know how to tell someone about abuse, sometimes because of vulnerability, disability or language barriers, and that this should not stop staff from being professionally curious and speaking to the designated safeguarding lead if they are worried.

Birmingham's four layers of need

Birmingham's multi-agency threshold guidance is called Right Help, Right Time and is published by the Birmingham Safeguarding Children Partnership. It describes four layers of need. The video shows them as rings, from green on the outside to red at the centre. The definitions below follow the current guidance (Version 7, June 2026).

  1. 1Universal needs (green)

    All children have a right to a range of services, such as health and education, and professionals make sure general needs are met.

  2. 2Universal Plus needs (yellow)

    The child and family need support above and beyond normal universal services. This is usually best organised by people who already know the child, such as a school or health professional, and can be done through an Early Help Assessment and an Our Family Plan.

  3. 3Additional needs (amber)

    The family may need an intensive or substantial package of support, which can still be met without statutory social work. A lead professional, usually someone already known to the family, coordinates the support through one plan.

  4. 4Complex or significant needs (red)

    The child's health or development may be impaired without services, or there is reasonable cause to suspect the child is suffering, or likely to suffer, significant harm. Child protection enquiries must be considered, and specialist services such as children's social care are accessed through the Children's Advice and Support Service (CASS).

A note on the video: it links the amber layer to an early help plan. In the current guidance, the Early Help Assessment and Our Family Plan are described at the Universal Plus layer, while the Additional layer is about a coordinated, multi-agency plan led by a lead professional. The knowledge check in the video gets the key idea right: a child who needs targeted support to stop problems escalating, without being at immediate risk, sits at Universal Plus.

When a child tells you something

The video teaches the TED approach for listening to a disclosure (when a child tells you about something that has happened to them). Use open prompts that let the child tell it in their own words.

  • Tell me what happened.
  • Explain what you mean.
  • Describe what you saw or heard.

The most important rule is never to promise to keep it secret. KCSIE is clear that staff should never promise a child that they will not tell anyone about a report of abuse, because this may not be in the child's best interests. Reassure the child that they are being taken seriously and that they will be supported and kept safe, then pass the information only to those who need it, such as your designated safeguarding lead.

The video also uses a short training case study, a seven-year-old called Leo who is showing signs of distress, to practise three steps: identify his needs, work out which layer of need applies, and plan the actions needed.

Online vulnerability

A child's online life can affect their safety and wellbeing offline. The video highlights cyberbullying, online grooming and the sharing of illegal content as harms with serious, long-term consequences that need a professional response. Birmingham's guidance asks practitioners to be aware of how a child may be vulnerable to, or experiencing, harm online, including through social media and messaging apps.

Recording and reporting

As the video puts it, if it is not written down, it did not happen. Stick to the facts, record the date, time and location, and use the child's own words rather than your interpretation. Then report to your designated safeguarding lead (DSL) straight away.

The KCSIE overview for all staff adds that you should act on any concern immediately, follow your setting's child protection policy, and make sure each record includes a summary of the concern, the actions taken, the decisions made, the reasons for those decisions and any outcomes. If a child is in immediate danger, call 999.

For practitioners in Birmingham, the Right Help, Right Time guidance (June 2026) gives the Children's Advice and Support Service as 0121 303 1888 (option 2, then option 2), from 8.45am to 5.15pm Monday to Thursday and 8.45am to 4.15pm on Friday. Outside those hours, the Emergency Duty Team is on 0121 675 4806. Always follow your own setting's procedures and speak to your DSL first unless a child is at immediate risk.

Why this matters for children and young people with SEND

KCSIE recognises that children with special educational needs or disabilities can face additional safeguarding challenges, both online and offline. The barriers it lists include assuming that signs of possible abuse, such as changes in behaviour, mood or injuries, are part of the child's condition without looking further, and these children being more likely to experience isolation or bullying. It also asks all school and college staff to be particularly alert to the potential need for extra support for a child who is disabled, or who has special educational needs, whether or not they have an EHC plan (education, health and care plan).

In practice, that means knowing each young person well enough to notice changes in behaviour, mood or attendance, giving them ways to communicate that suit them, and being curious rather than assuming a change is just part of their needs.

A quick checklist

  • Know who your DSL and deputy are, and how to reach them.
  • Know which threshold guidance applies where the child lives.
  • Listen, use TED prompts, and never promise to keep a secret.
  • Write down the facts, with the date, time, place and the child's own words.
  • Report to your DSL straight away, and call 999 if a child is in immediate danger.

Safeguarding is everyone's responsibility. Staying curious and understanding the thresholds of need helps make sure children get the right help at the right time.
